passages.t: ‘Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck’, and ‘zeal for Your house’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘Lilies.’ Of David” (verse 1). The first cry is short and desperate. “Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck” (verse 1). “I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing” (verse 2). He has cried until his throat is dry (verse 3).

He has many enemies, and no good reason for it. “Those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head” (verse 4). Yet he does not claim to be perfect. “You know my folly, O God, and my guilt is not hidden from You” (verse 5).

Much of his suffering comes from his faith. “For I have endured scorn for Your sake, and shame has covered my face” (verse 7). Even his family has turned away: “I have become a stranger to my brothers” (verse 8). Why? It is “because zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me” (verse 9).

When he mourns, people laugh. “Those who sit at the gate mock me, and I am the song of drunkards” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Deep water and mud were pictures of death. There was no place to stand and nothing to hold. The first hearers would feel the panic in the opening lines.

The gate of a town was its public square, where the leaders sat to judge cases. To be mocked at the gate was public shame before the whole town. Sackcloth, a rough cloth of goat hair, and fasting were signs of grief and of turning to God (verses 10 and 11). Here even his grief is made a joke.

The heading says “Of David”. Some readers place the psalm in one of the betrayals of David's life. Many scholars think the last verses, about rebuilding the cities of Judah, come from after the exile. The book page explains how readers weigh the headings.

Verse 5 matters. The psalmist admits ‘folly’ and ‘guilt’. He is not claiming to be sinless. He is saying he suffers for God's sake, not for his faults.
passages.later:
Beside Psalm 22, Psalm 69 is one of the psalms the New Testament uses most for the sufferings of Jesus.

When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, “His disciples remembered that it is written: ‘Zeal for Your house will consume Me’” (John 2:17, from verse 9). Paul quotes the second half of the same verse: “For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written: ‘The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me’” (Romans 15:3). Jesus said of those who rejected him, “They hated Me without reason” (John 15:25), words found in verse 4 and in Psalm 35:19.

Christians do not apply the whole psalm to Jesus. Verse 5 confesses guilt, and the New Testament says Jesus was without sin. The usual Christian reading is that David's sufferings were a pattern that Jesus filled out completely.
passages.hard: If the sinking and the shame in these verses describe how you feel, please hear this. Feeling as if you are going under is not a sign that God has left you. This psalmist felt it and kept praying. You do not have to pretend you are fine. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
‘Up to my neck’ is how many people feel at some point. The psalm does not tell you to calm down first. It starts with the cry: ‘Save me, O God.’ That is enough to begin with.

Verse 6 is a striking prayer: that his trouble would not make others lose heart. Even sinking, he thinks of other believers. Who might be watching how you hold on?

passages.t: ‘Answer me quickly!’, and ‘vinegar to quench my thirst’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm turns to prayer. “But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor. In Your abundant loving devotion, O God, answer me with Your sure salvation” (verse 13). “Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink” (verse 14).

He pleads with God not to turn away. “Hide not Your face from Your servant, for I am in distress. Answer me quickly!” (verse 17). “Draw near to my soul and redeem me” (verse 18).

Then he names the loneliness. “Insults have broken my heart, and I am in despair. I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one” (verse 20). Instead of kindness he got cruelty. “They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world, to share food and drink with someone in need was a basic duty. To put poison in a hungry man's food and give sour wine to a thirsty one was to betray that duty. It was hate dressed up as help.

‘Gall’ was a bitter, poisonous plant. ‘Vinegar’ here means sour wine, the cheap drink of soldiers and workers.

His prayer leans on God's character, not his own goodness. He asks God to answer by his ‘loving devotion’ and ‘great compassion’ (verse 16), the words God used of himself to Moses.
passages.later:
At the cross, the Gospels tell of Jesus being offered drinks. Matthew says that first “they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall; but after tasting it, He refused to drink it” (Matthew 27:34). Later, “One of them quickly ran and brought a sponge. He filled it with sour wine” (Matthew 27:48). John adds that Jesus said, “I am thirsty”, and then received the sour wine (John 19:28-30). The writers saw verse 21 in those moments.

Jesus also knew verse 20. In Gethsemane his friends slept, and at his arrest they ran.
passages.asks:
‘I looked for sympathy, but there was none’ is one of the loneliest lines in the Bible. If that is you, the psalm says two things. God is still the one to call on. And Jesus has been where you are.

The psalm also asks something of the rest of us. Be the comforter this psalmist could not find. Who near you is looking for sympathy?

passages.t: The curses of verses 22 to 28, and ‘I will praise God’s name in song’
passages.happening:
Now come some of the fiercest prayers in the Psalms. “May their table become a snare; may it be a retribution and a trap. May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever” (verses 22 and 23). “May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents” (verse 25). “May they be blotted out of the Book of Life and not listed with the righteous” (verse 28).

Then the tone changes completely. “But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God. I will praise God’s name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving” (verses 29 and 30). That praise pleases God “more than an ox” (verse 31). “For the LORD listens to the needy” (verse 33).

The psalm ends with the whole creation praising God, and with Zion and the cities of Judah rebuilt (verses 34 to 36).
passages.hearers:
The curses answer the cruelty before them. Those who poisoned his table should find their own table a trap. Those who would not see his pain should lose their sight. It is the language of justice that fits the crime.

‘The Book of Life’ was a picture of God's list of the living, like a roll of citizens. Moses once prayed, if God would not forgive Israel, “please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32). To ask that someone be blotted out is to ask God to remove them from his people.

The book page lists Psalm 69 among the cursing psalms and quotes verse 28.
passages.later:
The New Testament quotes these verses too, in a sober way. Peter applied verse 25 to Judas after his betrayal: “May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it” (Acts 1:20).

Paul quotes verses 22 and 23 in Romans 11:9-10, writing about those among his own people who did not believe in Jesus. He writes with grief, not scorn: “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2). And he says at once that this is not the end: “did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:11). The hardening is only “in part” and for a time (Romans 11:25). These verses give no one any reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people, and Paul himself warns his readers against pride (Romans 11:25).
passages.hard:
Here the two sides of Psalm 69 meet, and it is right to hold both honestly. The New Testament reads much of this psalm of Jesus. Yet these verses curse enemies, and at the cross Jesus prayed for the very people who were killing him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). How do readers handle that?

Most Christian readers do not put these curses in Jesus' mouth. They say the New Testament takes the psalmist's sufferings as a pattern for Jesus, but the curses remain David's own prayer. Jesus, the Son of David, prayed the opposite way. As Peter writes, “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate” (1 Peter 2:23). On this reading the contrast is the point.

Others read the curses as God's real judgment on those who finally reject him. On that reading the New Testament applies them not as personal revenge but as a sober warning, as Acts does of Judas.

The book page's part on the cursing psalms gives the wider readings: honest prayer that hands vengeance to God, the voice of the oppressed, prayers changed at the cross, and words not for Christian lips. Thoughtful believers hold each, and these notes do not choose. No reading makes it right to harm anyone.
passages.asks:
The psalm does not end in the curses. It ends in praise from someone still ‘in pain and distress’ (verse 29). He gives his anger to God and then turns to thanks.

If you are angry at people who have hurt you, this psalm shows a way: say it to God, all of it, and leave the judging with him. Then look at the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies. That prayer is the one Christians are finally asked to learn.
